act2.reliable: The whip's office has you down as reliable. Nobody says so, but the lines reach you a day earlier now, you get a question in the House, and your mentor stops introducing you as 'the new one'. You have a name. Act 2 is about making it stick.
act2.usefulTrouble: The whip's office has you down as trouble, the useful kind. You've voted against the line and lived, and people have noticed who stands up to the office. Your mentor says it's a reputation you can spend once. You have a name. Act 2 is about making it stick.

rival: {rival} came in with you, wants what you want, and has been counting the same vacancies. The whip's office has one assistant whip's chair to fill eventually. Only one of you gets it.

vacancy.open: {outgoing} is leaving the whip's office. There's a chair at the table and two names on the whip's desk: yours and {rival}'s. {whip} decides by the weekend. Your mentor and your clique will be asked.
vacancy.askMentor: Ask your mentor to speak for you
vacancy.askMentorNote: They'll spend some of what they have with the whip on you. They'll expect it back.
vacancy.askClique: Ask your clique to make the case
vacancy.askCliqueNote: The clique weighs in as a bloc. It costs you something with each of them.
vacancy.letItRunNote: No favours called in. The whip reads the file and decides.
vacancy.won: {whip} calls you in and keeps it short: the chair is yours. You answer for a row of fifteen now, and {rival} will remember that it wasn't them.
vacancy.lost: {whip} calls you in and keeps it short: it's {rival}'s. 'Next time,' they say, which is what they say. You can wait for the next vacancy, find a clique that will push harder for you, or take the committee chair the office is offering instead.
vacancy.waitNote: Keep your head down and your record clean. There will be another.
vacancy.changeCliqueNote: Join the caucus that likes you most. They'll push for you next time, and your old crowd will notice.
vacancy.committeeChairNote: A title, a staff and a say in what gets studied. The whip's office keeps your name on the list.

act3: You have a row. Fifteen members, some of whom you drank with as rookies, and a deputy whip who grades you on whether they turn up. Act 3 is about delivering people you don't outrank.

lottery.intro: The Clerk draws the private members' lottery and your name comes up. You get one bill of your own this Parliament. It needs a majority, which means votes from across the aisle, and the whip will want to know why you're talking to them.

crossAisle.intro: {bill} comes to a vote next week. Your own side will mostly let it through, but it needs opposition votes to pass. These three might be persuaded. You have time to ask {n} of them.

whipQuestion.intro: {whip} stops you in the lobby. 'I hear you've been across the aisle about your bill. Twice.' They wait.
whipQuestion.explainNote: It's your bill and it needs the votes. The whip won't like it, but they'll understand it.
whipQuestion.dropItNote: Withdraw the asks. The whip nods. The bill is probably dead.

ambition: {name} is running for the committee chair and has started counting heads. They mention, twice, that they'd remember who was with them.
{name} has been told the leader is watching them. They're trying to decide whether that's good news.
crisis: {name}'s spouse is in hospital in {riding}. They're flying back and forth and missing votes, and the whip's office has started to notice.
{name}'s family business has gone under. The paper hasn't got it yet. They've told almost nobody.
ridingTrouble: {name}'s riding association has called a meeting about them that they weren't invited to.
A plant in {riding} is closing and the town blames {name} for not stopping it.
retirement: {name} is sixty-seven and has started saying 'one more Parliament' in a way that sounds like a question.
lifeEvent.showUpNote: An evening of yours, spent on them. They'll remember it.
lifeEvent.ignoreNote: You have your own week. They'll notice you didn't.

act4: You run the count now. Every division goes through your board, every pair through your hands, and every whip on the other side knows your name. Act 4 is about who you trust across the aisle.
act5: The chair at the head of the whip's table is yours. You set the line with the leader, you hold the committee seats and the travel and the leave, and the caucus remembers everything you did to them on the way up. Act 5 is about what kind of whip you are.

leanOnFriend.intro: {name} came in with you. Their riding hates {bill}, and the line is {position}. The deputy whip wants them in their seat and voting it. It's your row.
leanOnFriend.gentleNote: Make the case, and let them know you'll remember it. It may not be enough.
leanOnFriend.hardNote: Remind them who decides their committee and their travel. They'll vote the line. They'll remember that too.
leanOnFriend.goNote: Some votes aren't worth a friend. The deputy whip will notice the gap.

demoted.soft: Your row went its own way on a vote that mattered, and the deputy whip has drawn the conclusion: you're soft. You're back on the backbench, with your friends and without the title.
demoted.bully: Your row went its own way on a vote that mattered, and the deputy whip has drawn the conclusion: nobody follows a bully. You're back on the backbench, and the row isn't sorry to see you go.
demoted.wrongCount: You said the count was safe. It wasn't, and the House knew it before the leader did. The Chief Whip has moved you sideways; you'll run a row again, if you can hold one.

confidencePair.intro: {bill} is a confidence vote next week and {absent} can't be in the House for it. {opposite}, {party}'s whip, is offering a pair. If it holds, neither counts. If it doesn't, you find out when the bells stop.
confidencePair.acceptNote: One fewer vote you need. One more thing that can go wrong.
confidencePair.declineNote: Nobody pairs with you; you get {absent} into the chamber or you don't.

temptation.intro: {leader} asks to see you. There's a parliamentary secretary's job going, with a car and a staff and, said without being said, cabinet beyond it. It would mean leaving the whip's office.
temptation.acceptNote: The whip's career ends here, with a record and an epilogue.

chiefVacancy.intro: {chief} is going to cabinet. The caucus has an opinion about who follows, and so does {leader}.
chiefVacancy.kept: {leader} went with {other}. You're still the deputy; you run the count, and you wait.

setLine.intro: {bill} is this week's question. With {leader}, you set the line.
setLine.whipNote: The caucus votes the line. Anyone who doesn't is in your book.
setLine.freeNote: Release the caucus. Loyalty rises; the result is theirs.
setLine.confidence: Make it a matter of confidence
setLine.confidenceNote: Everyone comes home for it. Lose, and the government falls.

cabinetOffer.intro: {leader} offers you cabinet. {portfolio}. It would end the whip's career, with everything you've done on the record.

fall.intro: The government fell on {bill}, and it was your count. {leader} has asked for your resignation as Chief Whip.
fall.stayNote: Start the climb again. The caucus remembers.

revolted.intro: Caucus turned on you. The leader didn't stop them.
revolted.stayNote: You know where the knives are now.

revolt.leader: {ringleader} stands up and says what half the room has been saying in the corridors: {leader} has lost the caucus. Hands go up. This is a revolt, and everyone is watching who sits still.
revolt.whip: {ringleader} stands up and says it to your face: the caucus is done being counted by you. Hands go up. Everyone is watching the head of the table.
revolt.backNote: Stand up for them. If the revolt fails, they'll remember. If it wins, so will the room.
revolt.joinNote: Put your hand up. If it wins, you helped; if it fails, you're marked.
revolt.won: The revolt carried. {leader} has stood down; {newLeader} leads the party now.
revolt.lost: The revolt failed. {leader} looked round the room and wrote some names down.
revolt.whipWon: The revolt carried. The room doesn't want you at the head of the table.
revolt.whipLost: The revolt failed. You're still the whip, and now you know who stood up.

ending.retirement: You chose your moment, which is more than most get. The House rose for a minute, and someone from your cohort said something kind and not quite true.
ending.cabinet: You took the oath on a grey morning and gave the whip's book to your successor, who will find your notes in the margins for years.
ending.exit: You took the car and the staff and the title. Cabinet was hinted at. It stayed hinted at.
ending.fall: The government fell on your count. You resigned before you were asked twice, and the paper spelled your name right.
ending.revolt: The caucus turned, and the leader let it. You left the whip's office with the book under your arm and nobody looking up.
ending.defeated: The riding decided. You watched the numbers come in at the association office with the lights half off, and the new member sent a gracious note that you did not answer for a week.
ending.nomination: The riding association held its meeting on a Tuesday night in the arena, and when the hands went up, they weren't for you. You watched someone else fight the election you'd prepared for.

replaced.intro: The leader's office has had enough. Lost confidence votes, public rebellions, a whip who couldn't deliver: {leader} has moved you out of the whip's office. You're on the backbench, and the pressure is off, which is its own kind of insult.
replaced.warn: The leader's office is watching. Another lost vote or a public rebellion and they'll find someone else to count.

agreement.signed: {gov} and {partner} sign a confidence-and-supply agreement: {partner} votes confidence for {weeks} weeks in return for movement on {category}.
agreement.broken: {partner} walks away from the confidence-and-supply agreement. "{gov} hasn't delivered," says {leader}. Every confidence vote is live again.
agreement.expired: The confidence-and-supply agreement with {partner} has run its course. Nobody is renewing it.

campaign.canvass: Five weeks of doors. Your feet hurt and the riding knows your face again.
campaign.tour: Five weeks on the leader's bus. You were in every photo and in none of the diners at home.
campaign.rest: The riding association ran it. They did fine. They know it.

office.1: The room you share: two desks, one window, a filing cabinet with somebody else's name on the drawers, and the boxes from the last member who sat here. Your deskmate works late too.
office.2: Your own door, with your name on it. One desk, one window, a bookcase with nothing on it yet. Visitors sit in the chair on the left.
office.3: The annex off the whip's office. The files for your row came up in two steel cabinets, and there's a coffee machine that someone will tell you is yours to keep topped up.
office.4: The deputy's room. Walnut, a rug, the party's flag in the corner and a board the size of a wall. Three cabinets of other people's secrets, and a chair for the ones who'd rather not sit across a desk.
office.5: The corner office. Two windows, the whips' table under the board, and the chair at the head of it. The sofa is for the conversations that aren't meetings.
